7.  Advancing Mental Health Care at the LAC+USC Medical Center

  Recommendation as submitted by Supervisor Solis: Establish and approve the
  LAC+USC Medical Center Ward 2E Remodel Project, Capital Project (CP) No.
  87863, with a total project budget of $6,522,000, and the LAC+USC Medical
  Center Wards 7A and 3D Remodel Project, CP No. 87864, with a total project
  budget of $22,406,000; approve the Fiscal Year (FY) 2022-23 appropriation
  adjustment to fund the FY 2022-23 estimated expenditures in the amount of
  $3,674,000 and $11,894,000, funded by the Behavioral Health Continuum
  Infrastructure Program grant, and the 10% match from the Department of
  Health Services (DHS) for the proposed CP Nos. 87863 and 87864,
  respectively; authorize the Director of Public Works to deliver CP Nos. 87863
  and 87864 using Board-approved Job Order Contracts; find that the proposed
  CP Nos. 87863 and 87864 are exempt from the California Environmental Quality
  Act; and authorize the Director of Health Services to take the following actions:
  4-VOTES

  Set up an Individual Development Bank Account (IDBA) jointly with
  Advocates for Human Potential, Inc., Behavioral Health Continuum
  Infrastructure Program grant and fiscal administrator;

  Make the necessary accounting transactions to initially transfer
  $3,319,000 in cash from DHS Designation and up to a total of
  $4,000,000, to the IDBA to fulfill the 10% County matching funds grant
  requirement;

  Designate three personnel to function as the IDBA Principals, and
  authorize the first IDBA Principal to request funding from the IDBA, the
  second IDBA Principal to approve funding payments, and the third IDBA
  Principal to send the payments from the IDBA to CP Nos. 87863 and
  87864 for reimbursement; and

  Execute periodic accounting transactions to draw down the grant funds
  and DHS match from the IDBA as actual expenditures are incurred by
  the capital projects and approved for reimbursement by Advocates for
  Human Potential. (22-4679)

9.  Phase Out of Oleoresin Capsicum Spray at Central Juvenile Hall

  Revised recommendation as submitted by Supervisors Solis and Horvath:
  Instruct the Chief Probation Officer to create an implementation plan, in
  collaboration with the Probation Oversight Commission (POC) and the Inspector
  General, to phase out the use of Oleoresin Capsicum (OC) spray, within 45
  days, at the housing units that incarcerate youth with developmental disabilities
  and girls and gender expansive youth at Central Juvenile Hall (CJH); authorize
  the Interim Director of Youth Development to expand the launch of the Credible
  Messenger Program Pilot (Program) to include Central Juvenile Hall and work
  with the Chief Probation Officer to implement the expansion in 60 days;
  authorize the Interim Director of Youth Development to execute and amend, if
  necessary, agreements not to exceed one year, plus one six month extension
  option to be exercised at the discretion of the Interim Director, to support the
  expansion of the Program, with a maximum contract amount for all of the
  agreements not to exceed $2,000,000, which will be fully supported by funds in
  the Department of Youth Development’s Fiscal Year 2022-23 budget; instruct
  the POC and the Inspector General to oversee the implementation and
  evaluation of the phase out of OC spray at CJH and report back to the Board in
  writing every 14 days, until the completion goal of February 3, 2023 including,
  at minimum, the following:

  The status and re-implementation of the Regional Center training and any
  additional trainings;

  How training is conducted and deployed, including the effectiveness of
  the “train the trainer” mode;

  The effectiveness of training in teams/units versus individuals;

  The impact of training on staff’s ability to de-escalate situations;

  The impact trained staff have on youth when de-escalation tactics are
  deployed; and

  Interviews with youth in CJH regularly, subject to their attorney’s consent,
  to determine accuracy of the Probation Department’s reporting;

  Instruct the Inspector General to track and collect data on staff who are
  engaging in multiple incidents of OC spray use, and in collaboration with the
  POC and the Chief Probation Officer, develop, review, and update policies on
  discipline and training regarding OC spray use;

10.  Reducing the Rate of Euthanasia on Animals in the Care of the
  Department of Animal Care and Control

  Recommendation as submitted by Supervisors Solis and Hahn: Instruct the
  Director of Animal Care and Control, in collaboration with rescue partners and
  animal welfare stakeholders, to report back to the Board in writing in 30 days
  with a full accounting of what led to the use of euthanasia on the 3-month-old
  puppy, Bowie, at the Baldwin Park Animal Care Center and a plan to prevent
  similar incidents; and report back to the Board in writing in 90 days with a
  five-year plan to decrease the number and percentage of animals who are
  euthanized with built-in, annual benchmarks, including the following:

  An accounting of the reasons for animals being euthanized including
  illness, safety, lack of rescue availability, etc., broken down by species
  and animal care center;

  A review of the Department of Animal Care and Control (DACC) policies
  and recommended changes that would help decrease the rate of
  euthanasia;

  An analysis of the feasibility of achieving a 90% live release rate;

  Gaps analysis to determine what resources and staffing may be needed
  to reduce the euthanasia rate;

  An assessment on the number of rescue and community partners
  needed to decrease the euthanasia rate without decreasing the number
  of intakes to animal care shelters;

  Recommendations for expanding and improving partnerships with
  rescues, fosters, and volunteers;

  A plan to expand prevention programs to minimize owner surrenders;

  An analysis of potential costs incurred by DACC to reduce the rate of
  euthanasia; and

15.  Establishing County Fair Workweek Employment Standards for Retail
  Workers

  Recommendation as submitted by Supervisors Mitchell and Horvath: Instruct the
  Director of Consumer and Business Affairs, through its Office of Labor Equity,
  in collaboration with the Director of Economic Opportunity, and the Interim
  County Counsel, to report back to the Board in writing in 120 days with the
  following:

  A summary of Los Angeles County’s current retail worker and industry
  landscape;

  An analysis of comparable local jurisdictions’ Fair Workweek policies’
  outcomes and lessons learned;

  An analysis of other worker groups or industries that could also benefit
  from the adoption of fair workweek policies; and

  Additional learnings from engagement of key relevant stakeholders such
  as employers, workers, labor, economic development, and
  community-based organizations;

  Instruct the Interim County Counsel, with support from the Directors of
  Economic Opportunity and Consumer and Business Affairs to return to the
  Board in six months with a Fair Workweek ordinance for adoption that would
  require all retail businesses in the unincorporated areas of the County with 300
  or more employees globally to do the following, as well as include anti-retaliation
  protections for employees exercising their rights under the ordinance, allow for
  the County to impose enforcement mechanisms, including restitution and
  penalties payable to the aggrieved employee:

  Provide employees with 14 days’ notice of their work schedule;

  Provide employees with the right to rest between multiple 10-hour shifts;

  Page 17

  Provide employees with a good faith estimate of weekly work hours at
  time of hire;

  Provide employees with a good faith estimate of potential opportunities
  for full-time work at time of hire;

  Provide employees with a good faith estimate of predictability of pay at
  time of hire;

  Provide employees with the right to request schedule changes and ability
  to decline hours before and after schedule posting;

  Ensure that additional work hours are offered to existing covered
  employees before hiring new workers; and

  Provide employees with predictability pay compensation for last-minute
  scheduling changes; and

  Direct the Chief Executive Officer, in consultation with the Interim County
  Counsel, and the Directors of Economic Opportunity and Consumer and
  Business Affairs to report back to the Board during the FY 2023-24 Final
  Changes budget phase with a cost estimate and a budget recommendation to
  implement the proposed Fair Workweek ordinance, to allow recommendations
  to be made within the context of the overall budget and numerous funding

18.  Fee Waiver and Gratis Issuance of a License Agreement for the
  Cornucopia Foundation's Malibu Farmers' Market held on certain Sundays
  at the Malibu Civic Center

  Recommendation as submitted by Supervisor Horvath: Find that the portion of
  the County’s Malibu Civic Center Parking Lot proposed for the farmers’ market
  is not currently needed for exclusive County purposes during those certain
  Sundays and those hours of operation of the Malibu Farmers' Market, to be
  defined in the license agreement; find that the services to be provided by the
  Cornucopia Foundation are necessary to meet the social needs of the County
  and serve public purposes which benefit the County; and take the following
  actions:

  Authorize the Chief Executive Officer to provide monthly non-exclusive,
  gratis day use permits to the Cornucopia Foundation, provided the
  Cornucopia Foundation is cooperating and providing the information the
  County needs to issue a license and the Cornucopia Foundation is not
  negatively impacting the County and public use of the Malibu Civic
  Center including, without limitation, the County public library, and
  provided such day permits do not extend past June 25, 2023;

  Waive the $175 per-day event fee and the $250 cleaning deposit fee,
  excluding the cost of security and liability insurance, for the day permits
  issued on certain Sundays;

  Authorize the Chief Executive Officer to execute other ancillary
  documentation necessary to effectuate the day use permits, and to take
  any other actions necessary and appropriate to implement and effectuate
